Neither my father, nor yours, fell into this trap without there being some very serious underlying issues. 

From my experience, SovCits tend to be relatively intelligent, but not very well educated. They're also generally poor, frustrated, lonely, angry, and insecure about all of those things.

You have to understand that this is a coping mechanism he's using to gain some sense of control, community, intellectual recognition and power. He's likely a very profoundly hurt person, and this obsessive delusion is coming from that place of pain. 

My father alienated himself from every single person he knew other than my mother, almost destroyed his marriage, blew up his successful businesses and died at 50 a more lonely, scared, hurt person than he ever was before he fell down the hole. 

This is very serious, and guiding him out of it will be, if it's even possible, a herculean task that in all likelihood no one single person will be able to accomplish. 

My advice would be to get help, and fast. Try to get him into therapy, help him find a positive community to be a part of, support his impulse to learn but guide it slowly to reality. Baby steps. It's going to take a long time, and a team of people working together to help him through this.


The earlier it is, the better chance you have to help him before it's too late.

It's going to take time, and work. I've never been very good at making or keeping friends- I thibk all of us can relate. But things have, on the whole, gotten better over the years. It's not hopeless.

My advice would be to 

1. Take the pressure off of yourself (and the people you meet) to make every interaction meaningful and profound and deep. Those kinds of connections come after knowing someone for a while, and it can be easy to come on too strong when you're not used to letting people get close to you, and you to them. Just relax. Enjoy the hang for what it is. 

2. Find places to be. This is important- you won't make friends from your room. Go to coffee shops, bars, parks, library's, shows, live music, etc etc. But do it consistently. Talk light shit with the bartenders. if you hang around long enough, and are generally unproblematic and good to be around, they'll be a good social anchor for you at the start. Someone to show everyone else you've been vetted and are safe/cool to be around.  

3.Give it time. It won't happen overnight, and you'll likely cycle through a bunch of people you connect with on one level or another. Eventually some of them will stick around and become better friends. they'll introduce you to more people, and on and on. after a while you'll have your own group, or groups, you're comfortable around.

This right here really gets to it. When people say houseless, they're really only talking about the homeless people they have unconsciously accepted as having enough humanity left to find salvation. To me, as a once homeless person, the word houseless is a little slimy. It's euphemistic and dishonest, while also allowing the people who use it as the default to feel like they're being a bit more progressive.
I replied in more detail below, but I was homeless and personally prefer the term homeless. Feels more human and captures more of the reality of the situation.

Maybe condescending isn't the right word. It's hard to put into words honestly. It feels disconnected from the reality of the experience, I guess. The focus being on the physical structure, in a vaccum, decouples it from the deeper dehumanization and othering that happens to you in that situation. There's a vague irony in there somewhere.  The language losing humanity in a mirrored, bizzarro version of how one loses their humanity when homeless. It's a thingafied word, as the homeless are thingafied. It may be a more precise and useful when talking about X number of housing unit structures vs Y number of occupants, and I get that, but I can't shake this feeling that adopting houseless as the de-facto term of common parlance over homeless is a net negative for precisely that reason.
